1031.event_title: Thailand revives the Royal Ploughing Ceremony
1031.event: Thailand's Royal Ploughing Ceremony, a rite of royal origin that marks the start of the rice-growing season, was suspended after 1936. The Cabinet revived it in 1960, King Bhumibol Adulyadej presided over it every year of his reign, and since 1966 the ploughing day has also been observed as National Farmers' Day.
1031.explanation: A modern state chose to honour the plough each year with its highest ceremony, at the head of the nation's calendar.
1031.tie_back: The kural says that however the world turns to other callings, it still follows behind the plough, and Thailand's crown and government still walk ceremonially behind it.
1031._accuracy_note: A symbolic rather than economic demonstration of the plough's primacy; it shows honour paid to farming more than dependence on it.

1032.event_title: Quesnay's Tableau economique names farmers the only productive class
1032.event: In 1758 Francois Quesnay, physician at the court of Louis XV, drew up the Tableau economique, a diagram of how wealth circulates through a nation. It divided society into landowners, a productive class of farmers and farm labourers, and a sterile class of artisans and merchants, holding that agriculture alone produced the net surplus on which all the others lived.
1032.explanation: The Tableau founded the Physiocratic school and is regarded as one of the first models of a whole economy.
1032.tie_back: The kural calls ploughmen the linchpin of the world because they bear everyone who does other work, and Quesnay's model made exactly that claim in economic form.
1032._accuracy_note: Quesnay's theory is almost a restatement of the kural; later economists rejected the idea that only agriculture is productive.

1033.event_title: Tao Yuanming gives up office to farm his own land
1033.event: The poet Tao Yuanming (Tao Qian) left his post as magistrate of Pengze in 405 after only a short term, and never returned to official service. He went back to his home to live as a farmer, and marked the decision with his poem Returning Home, which expresses his preference for poverty over the constraints of office.
1033.explanation: Tao became the model, for later Chinese poets and painters, of the person who prefers a hard but free life on the land to a comfortable post at someone else's beck and call.
1033.tie_back: The kural says those who plough and eat truly live while the rest eat by bowing to others, and Tao chose the plough over a life of bowing to superiors.
1033._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's contrast between ploughing to eat and bowing to eat, though Tao was a gentleman-farmer rather than a peasant.

1034.event_title: Li Bing builds the Dujiangyan irrigation system
1034.event: Around 256 BCE Li Bing, an official of the state of Qin governing the region of Shu, built the Dujiangyan system, which divides the Min River without a dam and distributes its water across the Chengdu Plain. It turned flood-prone land into fertile farmland, and it still irrigates more than 600,000 hectares today; it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2000.
1034.explanation: The farmland it watered became a source of grain for the Qin state, which went on to unify China in 221 BCE, and Sichuan has been known ever since as a land of abundance.
1034.tie_back: The kural says a realm rich in grain will see other kings' parasols bow beneath its own king's, and the abundance of the Chengdu Plain belonged to the state that later absorbed all its rivals.
1034._accuracy_note: The agricultural abundance is well documented; the link to Qin's later conquests is an interpretation and is kept out of the event field.

1035.event_title: Tolstoy ploughs for poor families on his estate
1035.event: In the 1880s Leo Tolstoy took up manual labour on his estate, and in August 1887 the painter Ilya Repin sketched him ploughing a field, a study now in the State Tretyakov Gallery. The Yasnaya Polyana museum notes that the field was where peasants had their allotments and that Tolstoy often ploughed for poor families who had no breadwinner.
1035.explanation: One of the world's most famous writers chose to live by the work of his hands and to give that work freely to those in need.
1035.tie_back: The kural says those who eat by the work of their own hands never beg and give to others without holding back, and Tolstoy's ploughing for the needy is a direct example.
1035._accuracy_note: Fits both halves of the kural, though Tolstoy was a wealthy landowner who chose manual work rather than depending on it.

1036.event_title: The Bardoli farmers withhold their revenue and the government gives way
1036.event: In 1928 the peasants of Bardoli taluka in Gujarat, led by Vallabhbhai Patel, refused to pay a sharply increased land-revenue assessment and held out in a disciplined, nonviolent campaign despite seizures of land and property. The campaign ended in success for the farmers, and Patel's leadership earned him the title Sardar.
1036.explanation: The campaign showed how much those in authority depend on the cultivators, and it made Patel a national leader.
1036.tie_back: The kural says that if farmers fold their hands even those who have renounced everything cannot stand, and Bardoli showed a government that could not stand firm once its farmers held back.
1036._accuracy_note: Next-best fit: it shows rulers' dependence on farmers, but the kural's point about ascetics depending on farmers' labour is not illustrated.

1037.event: Having seen vineyards in France and Italy where the earth between the rows was pulverised, Jethro Tull developed a horse-drawn hoe and applied the method on his own farm. In 1731 he published The New Horse Houghing Husbandry, which urged repeated working of the soil and caused controversy because Tull disapproved of using manure; Britannica notes that pulverising the soil did reduce the need for manure and improved aeration and water.
1037.explanation: Tull's methods, at first attacked, laid part of the foundation of modern British farming.
1037.tie_back: The kural says that soil worked and dried down to a fraction of its weight needs not a handful of manure, which is almost exactly what Tull set out to prove.
1037._accuracy_note: Tull's claim that well-worked soil needs little or no manure matches the kural closely, though his theory of why it worked was mistaken.

1038.event_title: Peru's guano becomes the world's most prized fertiliser
1038.event: From the early 1840s seabird guano from Peru's Chincha Islands was mined on a large scale and shipped to farms in Britain, Europe and the United States, where demand grew into what contemporaries called a guano mania. U.S. imports peaked at about 176,000 tons in 1854, and for decades guano supplied a major share of the Peruvian government's revenue.
1038.explanation: Farmers on several continents were willing to pay heavily for manure, showing how decisive fertilising had become to harvests.
1038.tie_back: The kural ranks manuring above ploughing, and the nineteenth-century world paid for Peruvian manure as though it were treasure.
1038._accuracy_note: Shows the high value placed on manure but not the kural's second claim about guarding crops.

1039.event_title: George Washington's daily ride around his Mount Vernon farms
1039.event: When in residence at Mount Vernon, George Washington made a daily inspection tour of his farms on horseback, a ride of around twenty miles, and his managers reported to him on the week's work every Saturday. When he was away, as during his presidency, he demanded detailed weekly written reports from his farm manager.
1039.explanation: Washington regarded the owner's constant personal attention as essential to a productive farm; the work itself was done largely by enslaved people.
1039.tie_back: The kural warns that land sulks like a neglected wife when its owner stays at home, and Washington made a point of going to his fields every day.
1039._accuracy_note: Illustrates the kural's advice by its positive side, the owner who goes to his land daily, rather than by an example of neglect.

1040.event_title: Yacouba Sawadogo turns barren land into forest with zai pits
1040.event: During a severe drought around 1980, farmer Yacouba Sawadogo began improving the traditional zai planting pits, making them wider and deeper and preparing them before the rains, on land that had been barren and abandoned. He created a forest of nearly 40 hectares with more than 60 species of trees and shrubs, and from 1984 held market days where farmers from many villages learned the technique.
1040.explanation: His work helped restore the productivity of tens of thousands of hectares in the region and earned him the Right Livelihood Award and the UN's Champions of the Earth award.
1040.tie_back: The kural says the Earth laughs at those who sit idle crying 'we have nothing', and Sawadogo showed that even land given up for dead would yield to effort.
1040._accuracy_note: A vivid example of effort drawing plenty from land others had abandoned, though the wider spread of zai involved many people besides Sawadogo.
